Z6_RT5Q7ff7aSilcCaKDtA.en: Weekly summary. Human cases: this week Cambodia reported one new human H5N1 influenza infection, and the United States reported one new fatal human H5N5 influenza infection. Animal outbreaks (WAHIS): three countries reported six new H5 (N untyped) outbreaks between 14 and 21 November 2025: Belgium 3, China 2, Portugal 1. Twenty-one countries reported 214 new H5N1 outbreaks between 14 and 21 November 2025: United Kingdom 60, Germany 35, Spain 22, Belgium 17, Nigeria 13, United States 9, Canada 8, Denmark and Finland 7 each, South Africa and France 5 each, Austria, Ireland, Latvia and Netherlands 4 each, Czechia, Switzerland, Luxembourg and Lithuania 2 each, and Norway and Portugal 1 each. The United Kingdom reported one new H5N5 outbreak on 21 November 2025. South Korea reported one new H5N9 outbreak on 19 November 2025. US dairy cattle infections: Cumulatively since March last year, 1,082 outbreaks have been reported across 18 states, mainly concentrated recently in Idaho. Human infections linked to cattle: at least 9,600 people have been monitored, 218 tested, and 41 positive (conjunctivitis, respiratory and influenza-like symptoms). Other spillover outbreaks: infections in domestic cats, sheep and alpacas, including a cat death. Wastewater surveillance: in week 46, 383 sampling sites provided test reports, and one state (New Jersey) had one sampling site detect H5-positive results. Other updates: In Grays Harbor County, Washington, a human H5N5 influenza infection was reported in November this year, and the patient died on 21 November. The patient was an elderly resident with chronic illness who kept multiple poultry at home and had been in contact with wild birds. Investigation indicates the infection most likely came from contact with the infected domestic poultry, bird droppings or a contaminated environment. The patient had high fever and breathing difficulties before admission, and after the rare H5N5 virus was confirmed, died from complications. This is the first confirmed human H5N5 infection globally to result in death. All close contacts have been traced and tested, and none tested positive; there is no evidence of human-to-human transmission, and the overall health risk to the general public remains low. Annual summary: Human cases this year: 2 H5 (including presumptive) influenza; 30 H5N1 influenza (992* cumulative since 2003); 1 H5N5 influenza (1 cumulative); 32 H9N2 influenza (162 cumulative); 2 H10N3 influenza (6 cumulative). Most cases had prior exposure to susceptible animals. *Per WHO statistics, US H5 influenza is classified as H5N1 cases. Avian and animal cases: 67 countries and areas have reported 4,299 highly and low pathogenic avian influenza outbreaks cumulatively. Assessment and recommendations: FAO, WHO and WOAH conducted a risk assessment of H5 viruses on 28 July. H5 viruses (clades 2.3.2.1a, 2.3.2.1e and 2.3.4.4b, among others) remain avian viruses. Human cases have mostly involved direct or indirect contact with susceptible animals or contaminated environments, and there is no human-to-human transmission capacity. Because the virus is widespread in wild and domestic animals, cases are expected to continue, and the global public health risk is assessed as low. The risk to the general public remains low, and low to moderate for people who frequently handle contaminated animals or environments, depending mainly on the mode and duration of contact, protection, and control measures. Authorities call for enhanced surveillance of susceptible animals and high-risk groups, avoiding drinking unpasteurized dairy products, and continued One Health cross-sectoral response measures.

hqNk0-usZN81JiN7yNtpHQ.en: Cambodia reported one new fatal H5N1 influenza case, a 22-year-old man living in Phnom Penh who died on 15 November after fever, cough and rapid or difficult breathing. This is the first confirmed case in the city. Epidemiological and genetic sequencing information has not yet been published, and the source of infection is still under investigation. Cambodia has cumulatively confirmed 18 infection cases this year, 7 of which were fatal. Cases in past years were mostly concentrated in southern provinces, but this year 31% of cases came from northern Siem Reap province. Before symptom onset, most cases had recent suspected or known contact with sick or dead birds, and no human-to-human transmission has been identified. The United States reported one new H5N5 influenza case, an elderly resident of Grays Harbor County, Washington, who has chronic illness and was admitted in early November with influenza-like symptoms (high fever, confusion and breathing difficulties); the patient remains hospitalized. The person kept poultry at home, and the poultry may have had contact with wild birds. Poultry or wild birds are most likely the source of transmission, and the source of infection is being clarified. gYPIZchdh6adZRMNWcJmMQ.en: Weekly summary. Human cases: the USA and Cambodia each reported one new human H5N1 infection this week. Animal outbreaks (WAHIS): 15 countries reported 166 new H5N1 outbreaks between 9 November 2024 and 27 February 2025: the USA 93, Germany 15, the Netherlands 14, Poland 11, South Korea 9, Hungary 7, Czechia 6, Denmark 3, Belgium 2, and Mexico, Italy, Sweden, Cambodia, Bulgaria and Canada 1 each. Australia reported one new H7N8 outbreak on 22 February 2025. Peru reported 12 new H5 (N untyped) outbreaks between 16 January and 13 February 2025. US dairy cattle avian influenza: dairy farms have reported 976 outbreaks cumulatively (3 new) in 17 states since March last year, recently concentrated in California, Nevada and Arizona. Human infections linked to cattle: at least 8,900 people monitored cumulatively, 217 tested, and 41 positive (conjunctivitis, respiratory and influenza-like symptoms). Other spillover: infections in domestic cats, sheep, alpacas and others, with cat deaths. Wastewater surveillance: in week 8, 389 sampling sites reported results, with H5-positive detections at 10 sites in 4 states. Other updates: the US has updated information on three recent human H5N1 infections. A dairy farm worker in Nevada had only conjunctivitis and has recovered. A worker at an Ohio poultry farm had taken part in culling operations at an avian influenza farm, and a patient in Wyoming had been exposed to poultry that died at home. Both of the latter patients were hospitalized with serious illness and have since been discharged. Specimens from the Nevada and Wyoming patients were genotyped as clade 2.3.4.4b (genotype D1.1), a genotype that has spread widely among wild birds and poultry and was recently detected in dairy cattle in Nevada and Arizona. Both patients' specimens showed a mutation in the PB2 protein associated with efficient replication in mammalian cells. The CDC says it has not yet found genetic changes affecting the effectiveness of antivirals or H5 candidate vaccines. Canada's Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) published a research report in February: in October last year, an H5N1 avian influenza variant resistant to oseltamivir (Tamiflu) was found on 8 poultry farms in British Columbia. The variant carries the H275Y mutation in the NA protein, which is very rare in clade 2.3.4.4b. The research team said the virus may have appeared in the country in late September last year. The USDA has designated the virus as genotype D1.1. Current evidence suggests the mutation may reduce viral fitness, yet the virus still spread rapidly to 8 poultry farms within 15 days. The research team recommends that influenza treatment strategies may need to be reassessed. Annual summary: 6 human H5N1 cases (914 cumulative since 2003), most with prior exposure to susceptible animals before onset. Avian and animal cases: 44 countries and territories have reported 907 highly and low pathogenic avian influenza outbreaks cumulatively. Assessment and recommendations: FAO, WHO and WOAH published a risk assessment on H5 influenza viruses on 20 December. H5 2.3.4.4b viruses are still avian viruses; human cases have generally involved direct or indirect contact with susceptible animals, and there is no human-to-human transmission capacity. Because the virus is widespread in wild and domestic animals, cases are expected to continue, and the global public health risk is assessed as low. The risk is low for the general public, and low to moderate for people who often handle contaminated animals or environments, depending mainly on the type and duration of exposure, protection and control measures. Countries are urged to strengthen surveillance of susceptible animals and high-risk groups.
